The reasonableness of transferring the cost implication without commensurate benefits to the beneficiaries needs to be seen in the context that the beneficiaries also do not have any control over coal_ 2. Aggrieved by the said order, the Petitioner, NTPC, filed Appeal No. 399 of 2019 before the Hon’ble Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL), inter alia, seeking setting aside of the Commission’s order dated 28.8.2019 and relaxation of NAPAF for FYs 201718 and 2018-19 by treating the shortfall in availability due to non-availability of coal as deemed generation for recovery of fixed charges. The Hon’ble APTEL, vide judgment dated 13.1.2026 in Appeal No. 399 of 2019, set aside the Commission’s order dated 28.8.2019, observing as under: 3. On 24.4.2026, the learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that the Hon’ble APTEL, vide Judgment dated 13.1.2026 in Appeal No. 399 of 2019, had remanded the matter to the Commission with a direction to reduce the NAPAF from 85% to 83% for the specified thermal generating stations for the period from 1.4.2017 to 31.3.2019 for recovery of fixed charges. The parties sought time to file written submissions, which was granted, and the matter was listed for hearing on 21.5.2026. On 27.5.2026, the Petitioner submitted that MSEDCL had filed a Civil Appeal before the Hon’ble Supreme Court against the APTEL Judgment and, in the absence of any interim order, requested the Commission to proceed with the matter subject to the outcome of the proceedings before the Hon’ble Supreme Court. MPPMCL also sought time to file its submissions, stating that it was in the process of filing an appeal. The Commission directed the Petitioner to furnish, on affidavit, additional information and the status of the proceedings before the Hon’ble Supreme Court. The Respondents were permitted to file their replies by 15.7.2026 and the Petitioner its rejoinder by 22.7.2026. The matter was thereafter listed for hearing on 28.7.2026. On 30.7.2026, the learned counsels for the Petitioner and the Respondents made detailed submissions and reiterated their respective pleadings. After hearing the parties at length, the Commission reserved the matter for order. 8. MPPMCL, vide affidavit dated 15.7.2026, mainly submitted that the Hon’ble APTEL had found that NTPC failed to establish that the Government of India directives dated 20.10.2015, 3.5.2017 and 4.5.2017 materially affected coal availability and also failed to establish the efforts undertaken for optimal utilisation of available coal to enhance Plant availability and achieve the normative NAPAF. MPPMCL further submitted that it had filed Civil Appeal (Diary No. 29878 of 2026) before the Hon’ble Supreme Court on 13.5.2026, challenging the APTEL Judgment on the issue of relaxation in NAPAF, and requested the Commission to undertake appropriate prudence check of NTPC’s claim for additional fixed charges, including verification of the station-wise and beneficiary-wise impact, subject to the final outcome of the said Civil Appeal. 9. The Petitioner, in its rejoinder affidavit dated 22.7.2026, mainly submitted that the Commission had already granted the same relaxation of NAPAF from 85% to 83% for the period from 1.4.2017 to 31.3.2019 in respect of Vallur Thermal Power Station, pursuant to the Hon’ble APTEL’s Judgment dated 8.4.2025 in Appeal No. 318 of 2019, which has attained finality. NTPC further submitted that it had furnished the station-wise data and computations sought by the Commission and that MPPMCL could not seek reconsideration of the findings of the Hon’ble APTEL before the Commission. It stated that MPPMCL’s remedy, if any, lies before the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the Civil Appeal filed by it, in which no interim order has been passed. 10. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner and the Respondents, the additional information furnished by the Petitioner, the rejoinder and the relevant provisions of the Tariff Regulations, 2014. The issue for consideration is limited to implementation of the judgment dated 13.1.2026 of the Hon’ble APTEL in Appeal No. 399 of 2019. 12. The Respondents have submitted that appeals against the judgment dated 13.1.2026 are pending before the Hon’ble Supreme Court and that the consequential recovery should be subject to the outcome thereof. It is, however, not disputed that no interim order or stay against the operation of the said judgment has been granted by the Hon’ble Supreme Court. Therefore, the judgment of the Hon’ble APTEL continues to operate and is required to be implemented. The pendency of the Civil Appeals, in the absence of any order staying the judgment, does not preclude its implementation. 13. The PAF furnished by the Petitioner indicates that all four generating stations had PAF below 85% during FY 2017-18, whereas during FY 2018-19 only Mouda Stage-II had PAF below 85%.
